build: Mirrorsoft's 1991 disk release, speedball_2[mirrorsoft_1991].g64 from the C64 Preservation Project's 10th Anniversary Collection on the Internet Archive (SHA-256 c379e7c1…4dc4)

exclude: zero page: the game's variables, zeroed by new_game_state and set before use; at the start it still holds the loader's unpacker, which never runs again
the sound driver's state, seven bytes a voice in each of its tables, set by sfx_init and sfx_play before use
the game's variables: the objects' positions, the players' attributes, the league, cup and statistics, zeroed by new_game_state or set before use
after the portrait tiles: the block map of the arena and the portraits' mirror bits, unpacked there before use
zeros after the MARTIN picture, never read
zeros after the title routine, never read
the bitmap, the arena's screens and characters and the menus' sprites, all unpacked or drawn there before use; at the start it holds what the load left

comments.text: Silences the sound-effects driver: marks no effect requested on the three voices ($04B0, $04B7, $04BE = $FF), sets their running priorities ($04DE, $04E5, $04EC) to $FF so that any effect may start, zeroes their length and hold counters, clears all 24 SID registers ($D400-$D417) and sets the volume to 15 with no filter ($D418 = $0F).

The sound-effects driver's frame step: runs sfx_voice for voice 1 (X = 0), voice 2 (X = 7) and voice 3 (X = 14), the offset of each voice in the SID and in the driver's own state at $04B0. Called from the raster interrupts' end-of-frame handlers ($1446, $1452), the sound-only interrupt at $1463, sfx_stop_all ($1C12) and three more places ($2062, $75B7, $C101).

One voice of the sound-effects driver, X = the voice's offset (0, 7, 14). A request waits in $04B0,x (bit 7 set means none). It starts when the voice's hold counter $04B1,x is zero or when the effect's priority byte (sfx_priority) is no higher than the running effect's ($04DE,x): a lower number wins. Otherwise the request is dropped. Starting an effect gates the voice off, then copies the effect's four-byte rows from the tables at $04FE-$0741 into the voice: attack/decay, sustain/release, gate time, length, waveform at start and after the gate, frequency, frequency-sweep mode and step, pulse width, pulse sweep, special effects and their period; the hold counter is set to 50 frames. A running effect goes on at sfx_step.
kernal_on writes 0 to $02A1, the KERNAL's RS-232 interrupt flags, after copying this page away; here the bytes are the sound driver's code (sfx_step), put back by kernal_off.
A false symbol: the BIT at $65C1 skips the two-byte instruction inside it; no instruction names $02A9, which lies in sfx_voice.

A running effect's frame (sfx_voice jumps here, X = the voice). Counts the hold counter down and toggles the flip flag $04DF,x every $04DC,x + 1 frames. While the gate time $04E0,x lasts it counts down; once it is out the voice switches to its release waveform (gate off), then the length $04B2,x counts down to silence unless it is $FF (endless). Then: pulse-width sweep between $08xx and $0Exx when $04CA,x is set; the frequency sweep chosen by $04C5,x (1 up, 2 down, 3 up while gated, 4 down while gated, 5 up then down at release, 6 down then up, 7 up after release, 8 down after release, 9 up or down with the flip flag); and the special bits of $04DA,x: 1 swap the frequency's two bytes, 2 subtract the step's high byte $04C6,x from the frequency's high byte and EOR it with $04DD,x, 4 add the low nibble of voice 3's oscillator ($D41B AND $0F) to the high byte for noise, 8 reset the high byte to $04DD,x when the flip timer runs out.
kernal_on copies the page from here ($0300-$03FF, the sound driver's code) to $E600 before handing the machine to the KERNAL, and kernal_off copies it back.
kernal_on and load_game set the KERNAL's interrupt vector at $0314-$0315 here once the page is saved; the bytes are the sound driver's, put back by kernal_off.
The high byte of the KERNAL's interrupt vector, set with $0314.
kernal_on sets the KERNAL's NMI vector at $0318 here once the page is saved; the bytes are the sound driver's, put back by kernal_off.

Each sound effect's priority, one byte for each of the 48 effects (0-47): a new effect replaces a running one when its byte is no higher. Mostly 3, with 2 for the effects that must be heard. Read by sfx_voice ($024B, $026B).
A false symbol: BIT $04A9 at $1488 is the two-byte-skip idiom (it hides the LDA #$04 at $1489 when $1486 runs), not a read of this table. sfx_priority runs on to $04AF here.

The 48 sound effects' parameters, six interleaved tables of four bytes per effect (effect number times 4 indexes them), read only by sfx_voice: $04FE attack/decay, $04FF sustain/release, $0500 gate time in frames, $0501 length after the gate ($FF endless); then (at $05BE) waveform at start, waveform after the gate, frequency high and low; (at $067E) frequency-sweep mode, sweep step high and low, pulse width (high nibble the low byte, low nibble the high byte); (at $073E) pulse-sweep step, special-effect bits, flip period and the value the special effects use. Effect 0 is all zeros.
The second column of sfx_params: each effect's sustain and release (SID register 6), four bytes apart.
The third column: how many frames each effect's gate stays on.
The fourth column: how many frames each effect runs after the gate, $FF for endless.
A false symbol: the BIT at $2BF2 skips the two-byte instruction inside it; no instruction names $05A9, which lies in sfx_params.

Second group of sfx_params, four bytes per effect: the waveform and gate written at the start ($05BE), the waveform after the gate time ($05BF), the start frequency's high byte ($05C0) and low byte ($05C1).
The second column of the second group: the waveform after the gate.
The third column: the starting frequency, high byte.
The fourth column: the starting frequency, low byte.
The waveform and frequency rows of sfx_waves go on here (an index into the table at $05F7 is how one reader names it); the group ends at $067D.
Third group of sfx_params, four bytes per effect: frequency-sweep mode (0 none to 9, see sfx_step), sweep step high and low, and the pulse width packed as two nibbles.
The second column of the third group: the frequency sweep's step, high byte.
The third column: the sweep's step, low byte.
The fourth column: the pulse width, its low byte in the high nibble and its high byte in the low nibble.
The rows of sfx_sweeps go on here; the group ends at $073D.
More rows of sfx_sweeps, to $073D.
sfx_params' pulse widths for effects 43-47 (the end of the third group).

Fourth group of sfx_params, four bytes per effect: pulse-sweep step (0 for none), special-effect bits (see sfx_step), the flip period less one, in frames, and the value the special effects use as a frequency or a mask.
The second column of sfx_specials: which special effects the effect uses (sfx_step).
The third column: the flip period less one, in frames (the flag toggles every value + 1 frames).
The fourth column: the value the special effects use as a frequency or a mask.
1 while the game is paused with the P key (match_frame); match_setup clears it.
How near (column plus row distance) an opponent may come before a computer ball carrier dodges or passes: 3, or 6 when the computer plays both teams. Set by match_setup.

A small font of 3-pixel-wide glyphs, two rows of a glyph packed in each byte as nibbles, four bytes a glyph, read by the bitmap text printer at $508B-$5280. The order follows the screen codes the game prints: letters first, then digits and punctuation.
mini_font's second byte of each character, read by print_char_tall with the first, third and fourth.
mini_font's third byte of each character, for print_char_tall.
mini_font's fourth byte of each character, for print_char_tall.
The rest of mini_font: digits, punctuation and a few symbols, to $0D10.
mini_font's characters from $3C on.

Each of the 16 teams' overall strength for a match between two computer teams (simulate_match): Brutal Deluxe $64, then $70 up to $E2 for Super Nashwan. The rows of team_ratings follow on, and $5CBE reads the two as one table, 16 bytes a team from here.

The ratings of teams 1-15, 16 bytes a team, two 4-bit digits a byte: eight attributes (AGR, ATT, DEF, SPD, THR, POW, STA, INT) for each of the three groups of three players, then eight for the substitutes. An attribute is 100 + 10 x digit (team_2_ratings).

The 16 teams' names in ASCII capitals, each ended by a zero byte: BRUTAL DELUXE, REVOLVER, RAW MESSIAHS, VIOLENT DESIRE, BAROQUE, THE RENEGADES, DAMOCLES, STEEL FURY, POWERHOUSE, RAGE 2000, MEAN MACHINE, EXPLOSIVE LORDS, LETHAL FORMULA, TURBO HAMMERS, FATAL JUSTICE, SUPER NASHWAN. Then the players' names to $0F80: BARRY, COLIN, JUSTIN, NIGEL, DARREN, GRAHAM, ARNOLD, ROBIN, TREVOR, STUART, GORDON, KEVIN, SHORN, QUISS, ROCCO, LUTHOR, WEISS, CAZA, ROSCOP, QUAID, MONTEZ, COOPER, GARRIK, NORMAN, JENSON, JAMS.
The players' names go on (WEISS's last letter, CAZA, ROSCOP, QUAID, MONTEZ, COOPER, GARRIK, NORMAN, JENSON, JAMS); $6483 and $6D06 index the table from here.
Rows of five bytes for the star players on the transfer market: a flag byte, then four bytes of packed 4-bit attributes. Read at $652E and $653A.

Unpacks the routine packed straight after the JSR that called it to $C000 and runs it there: takes the return address off the stack as the packed data's start, calls unpack ($498E) to write from $C000, then jumps to $C000 with A and Y as the caller left them. The packed routine's own RTS returns to the caller of the routine that called run_packed. Called at $534C, $5431, $559B and $764A, each followed by its packed bytes.
An RTS nothing jumps to, between run_packed and the panel split's delay table.

How many delay loops the score panel's raster split waits before switching the video mode, one byte for each of the eight vertical scroll positions ($7A, the pitch's $D011 scroll), so that the switch lands at the same place on the screen. Read at $100C; the second split at $1035 reads the eight bytes from $0FF3.
The second half of panel_d011's table: the values irq_panel_low loads by Y.
The $D011 value the score panel's split writes for each vertical scroll position: $5F for most (bitmap off, extended colour off, 25 rows, scroll 7), $5E for two. Read at $1013.
The last three values of panel_d011.

Raster command $82 (raster_commands): the score panel's split. Waits for raster line $DC, waits the delay panel_delays gives for the pitch's vertical scroll, sets the panel's scroll ($D011 from panel_d011), screen and characters ($D018 = $CC: screen $F000, characters $D800 in bank 3), 38-column scroll off ($D016 = $18), and its colours: background black, $D022 and $D023 from $5E and $5F.

Raster command $83: a second split for the panel, lower down. Waits for raster line $E4 and the delay from $0FF3, then sets $D011 = $1F (screen on, 25 rows); returns through the multiplexer's next-entry step.

Sets up the sprite multiplexer for a match: clears the raster list's buckets at $0100, puts the raster commands $81 at the top (pitch), $82 (panel split) at bucket $36, $83 at $38 and $84 (end of frame) at $3A, marks buckets $36-$3F used, points the IRQ vector at $126B and starts the raster interrupt at line $23 through irq_enable. Called at $2911.
Turns on the raster interrupt ($D01A = 1), acknowledges any pending one, resets the multiplexer's list positions ($05, $07, $08) and sets the first interrupt at line $23.

Sets up the multiplexer for the menus and managers' screens: list length $3F, sprite pointers through $CFF8 (the store at $1299 patched to $CF), camera at zero, the raster list cleared with command $85 at the top and $86 at bucket $3F, and the IRQ vector at $1300 (the multiplexer with per-sprite multicolour and expansion); then irq_enable.
A false symbol: the BIT at $2C72, $4C37 skips the two-byte instruction inside it; no instruction names $10A9, which lies in mux_menus.
Points the IRQ vector at irq_sfx ($1463), which only plays sound effects, and starts the raster interrupt with irq_enable. Used while a screen is unpacked or drawn.
Rebuilds the multiplexer's raster list with no colour-change line: clears buckets 1-$3E, then sorts as mux_sort does.

Sorts the visible objects into the raster list for the next frame, with interrupts held off. Clears buckets 1-$35, puts command $88 (a colour change) at bucket $08 when it is set, then for each of the 26 objects (X = 0-$19) whose flag at $A0,x has bit 0 set: converts its pitch position ($0800/$E6 down, $0180/$CC across) less the camera ($7F/$80, $7D/$7E) into a sprite's Y (+$32) and X (+$18, with the ninth bit), keeps them with its colour ($0834) and frame ($081A) in the slot tables at $0A20-$0A88, and drops its slot number in the first free bucket at or above its line / 4, skipping objects above line 20. Finally compacts the used buckets, in order, into the list at $0140 the interrupt walks.

Places up to eight objects straight into the video chip's sprite registers, without the multiplexer: the same position sums as mux_sort, writes $D000-$D00F, $D010, colours and the frame to both sets of sprite pointers ($CFF8 and $F7F8), parks the unused sprites at Y = $FA, and leaves a raster list of only the commands ($88 if set, then $36, $38, $3A). Called at $20B0.

The raster interrupt in a match: the sprite multiplexer. Takes the list entry for this line from the bucket table at $0100: an object's slot number moves the next of the eight hardware sprites in turn to that object's Y, X, frame (into the sprite pointers, high byte patched at $1299), colour and ninth X bit; a byte with bit 7 set is a raster command (raster_commands). Then (mux_next) steps to the next list entry and sets $D012 to its line (bucket times 4); when that line has passed already it handles the entry at once by jumping back in past the register saves (the vector plus 5).
The interrupt routines write the next raster line's sprite registers into the operands of the instructions here (the operand at $1299), which mux_next then runs.

The multiplexer's step to the next raster-list entry, shared by every raster command: reads the entry's bucket from $0140, programs $D012 for line bucket*4 and returns from the interrupt, or runs the entry at once when the line has gone.
A raster-list entry with bit 7 set: its low nibble (0-8) indexes raster_commands, and the handler is jumped to through $2B. Entries 9-15 are skipped.
Five bytes nothing runs: LDA #$00 / STA $D01A, which would turn the raster interrupt off.
Restores Y, X and A and returns from the interrupt.
The next entry's line has passed: re-enter the interrupt handler five bytes in (past its pushes), through the vector at $FFFE.

The multiplexer for the menus and managers' screens (vector set by mux_menus): as irq_mux, and also sets each sprite's multicolour bit (on for colour 2, off otherwise) and doubles its size in both directions for colour 15 (the gym's player figure).

The raster-list commands $80-$88, as addresses of their handlers: $80 nothing, $81 pitch top ($139F), $82 panel split ($1003), $83 low panel split ($1035), $84 end of frame ($141F), $85 menus' top ($13BC), $86 menus' end of frame ($1452), $87 pitch top without parking the sprites ($13ED), $88 colour change ($1397).
The high bytes of raster_commands' addresses.
Raster command $80: does nothing and steps on.
Raster command $88: sets multicolour 2 ($D023) from $5D partway down the screen.

Raster command $81, the top of the pitch: sets the vertical and horizontal scroll ($7A, $7B, with the screen on and 38 columns), the three background colours from $5A-$5C, then parks all eight sprites at Y = $FA and chooses the screen being shown (irq_screen).

Raster command $85: parks the eight sprites below the screen and shows one of the two screens: with $7C zero, $D018 = $3E (screen $CC00) and sprite pointers at $CFF8; otherwise $D018 = $DE (screen $F400) and pointers at $F7F8. The pointer page is patched into irq_mux's store at $1299.
Raster command $87: as irq_pitch_top without parking the sprites.

Raster command $84, the end of a match frame: resets the raster list to its top and the next interrupt to line $23, counts the frame in $43, and with interrupts back on runs the game's frame, match_frame ($2052), unless the last one has not finished ($09) or bit 7 of $45 asks for sound only, when it plays the sound effects instead and takes the frame back out of $43.
Raster command $86, the end of a menu frame: plays the sound effects and resets the raster list to line $23.
An interrupt handler that only plays the sound effects and acknowledges the video chip (set by irq_sound_only).

The camera check (camera_check) when bit 6 of $45 is set, the camera following a fixed point: tests whether the followed object ($60) is more than $12 columns right of the camera or $0A rows below it, and starts the scroll with those directions; otherwise no scroll ($86 = 0).

Decides whether the pitch must scroll to keep the followed object ($60, normally the ball) in view. Not while a scroll is running ($88). Compares the object's place, less the camera's, with a window ($10-$18 across, $13-$15 when already moving sideways; $08-$0B down) and builds the directions in $87: 1 up, 2 down, 4 left, 8 right, as far as the pitch's edges allow ($7E 3-$26 across, $80 3-$80 down). With a direction it goes on at camera_step, otherwise clears $86.

Chooses the scroll's speed: $83 (0-3) indexes the windows at camera_windows; the scroll speeds up a step, up to 3, while the object stays outside the window for its speed, and each faster speed's window is wider.

Advances a scroll of the pitch by a step of one pixel in the directions in $87, over nine frames a character: on the first it works out the new camera character position ($84 across, $85 down) and which fine scroll positions ($81, $82) roll over, on the fifth flags ($8A) that the new row or column must be drawn, and on the ninth makes the new position the camera's and checks again (camera_check). Each frame it moves the fine scroll ($81, $82) a pixel unless that axis has finished.

Four speeds' windows for camera_step: column limits ($1678 left, $167C right) and row limits ($1680 top, $1684 bottom) around the followed object, wider as the scroll speeds up: columns 13-27, 10-30, 6-34, 6-34 and rows 6-13, 4-15, 2-17, 2-17.
The second byte of each camera window (camera_windows), read by camera_step.
The camera's vertical windows, read with $1684 by camera_step for its rows.
The second byte of each vertical window.

Builds the pitch's lookup tables: 38 row addresses of the block map at $BCEF (20 bytes a row) into $0920 (low) and $0946 (high), and 90 block addresses at $96BC (16 bytes a block, 4 by 4 characters) into $096C and $09C6. Called at $273B and $29DF.

Draws the pitch after a scroll by a whole character. When the camera moved by at most one character on each axis it shifts the visible screen by patching the screen-copy routine at $7A51 (its source and destination offsets and screen page, $F4 or $CC for the hidden screen) and runs it (pitch_copy, $7A4F); otherwise it draws all 22 rows afresh from the block map (row by row through pitch_row_bytes into $E4D0, 40 characters a row) and turns the pitch's characters for the half the camera is in (mirror_chars).
Draws the new top row after a scroll up: decodes the row from the block map into $E4D0 and copies its 40 characters to the hidden screen's first row ($F400 or $CC00, by $7C).
Draws the new bottom row after a scroll down, into the hidden screen's row 21 ($F748 or $CF48).
Draws the new left column after a scroll left: decodes the column (pitch_column_bytes) and stores its 22 characters down the hidden screen's first column.
Draws the new right column after a scroll right, into column 39 of the hidden screen.

Decodes one screen row of the pitch into the buffer $E4D0 (40 characters): A = the row; works out the block row (A / 4) and the line in the block (A and 3), the block column from the camera's column $84, then for 12 blocks across copies four characters from each block's definition.
Decodes one screen column of the pitch into $E4D0 (22 characters): A = the column; walks seven blocks down from the camera's row $85, four characters from each.

The drawing half of a scroll by a character: turns the characters of the half of the pitch the camera has crossed into (mirror_chars, from $E536) and draws the new row or column at the side the camera moved to. Then sets $8B to 2 (draw done) unless it is 3.

Turns four characters of the pitch's set at $F800 upside down: X = a group number; swaps the bytes 0 and 7, 1 and 6, 2 and 5, 3 and 4 of each of characters 4X to 4X+3 that lie between $80 and $FE. The two halves of the arena use the same characters, one half drawn upside down; the flags at $E536 say which groups are turned now.

Colours the score panel: sprite pointers of the panel screen ($F3F8) to $BF (an empty frame), colour RAM rows $DB70-$DBE7 light blue, the white parts ($DB9A-$DB9C, $DBBB-$DBBD, $DBAB, $DBAC), the team colours from $1D40 and from the table at $1D3C by $3D.
A false symbol: the BIT at $458C, $45AC skips the two-byte instruction inside it; no instruction names $1AB1, which lies in panel_colours.

Writes the two scores and the clock into the score panel's screen ($F39A-$F3BD): each score is three decimal digits ($47/$49/$4B for team 1, $48/$4A/$4C for team 2), shown as 999 when the hundreds pass 9; the clock $4D is two BCD digits at $F3AB. Then the two energy bars (panel_bar for the players $72 and $73) and the marker under the controlled player ($60) in colour RAM, from panel_marker_cols.
The colour RAM column of the panel marker for each of the 18 players (three bytes each for six positions), read at $1B2D and $1B3A. The 19th byte, $1B55 ($50), is past the table and nothing reads it.

Draws a player's energy bar in the panel: Y = the player; reads his energy at $08DE,y (a fixed value when Y is $12 or more). Each of the bar's first three cells at $F3A0,x shows full (character $12) when the energy reaches 64, 128 and 192, otherwise empty ($0A), and the fourth starts empty; it returns in Y the cell the energy ends in (energy / 64) and in A the part-filled character for it, $0A plus (energy / 8) mod 8, which the caller stores there.
Adds A (a BCD bonus) to team X's score: keeps a running count in $0C09,x and adds the value to the decimal digits through score_add_bcd.
Adds the BCD byte A to team X's three-digit score: units $47,x, tens $49,x, hundreds $4B,x, carrying by tens; the hundreds stop at 255.
Takes A from team X's score (adds its tens' complement in BCD), and clears the score to zero when it would go below.
Requests sound effect A on voice 1 and clears voice 2's request: the usual way the game plays an effect.
Requests sound effect A on voice 3.
Requests effect A on voice 1 and effect A+1 on voice 2: the two-voice effects.
Clears the three voices' requests to effect 0 and runs the driver once, so that every voice stops.
The eight bit masks 1, 2, 4 ... $80: a sprite's bit in the VIC's registers, and a key's column in the keyboard scan.
The eight masks with one bit clear ($FE ... $7F): a sprite's bit cleared, and a keyboard row selected in $DC00.
The masks that clear one multicolour pixel of a byte, left to right ($3F, $CF, $F3, $FC), for plot.
Each 4-bit nibble with every bit doubled into a pixel pair ($00, $03, $0C, $0F ... $FF): the mini font's rows as multicolour pixels.
The matches in a two-player series for each choice of menu 1: 1, 3 and 5.
The direction (0 up, 1 up-right ... 7 up-left) for each combination of the joystick bits (1 up, 2 down, 4 left, 8 right), $FF for none or an impossible one.

The keys that stand in for joystick port 2 (read_input), as key numbers: I (up), M (down), J (left), K (right), SPACE (fire) and RUN/STOP; the seventh entry the loop reads is the next table's first byte, A.
The keys for joystick port 1: A (up), Z (down), comma (left), full stop (right), / (fire) and RUN/STOP; the seventh read is $C0 from the next table.
The bitmap address of each text row for print_big, low bytes ($1C59) and high bytes ($1C60): seven rows from $E3C0.
The high bytes of big_text_rows.
Seven more bytes after the text rows' high bytes ($4A to $DA in steps of $18) that nothing reads.
What a goal is worth to team 1 for each multiplier position (0-4), in decimal: 20, 15, 10, 10, 10 (multiplier_points). An injury the team causes and a row of five stars are worth the same.
What a goal is worth to team 2: 10, 10, 10, 15, 20.
What a star or a dome is worth to team 1: 4, 3, 2, 2, 2.
The same for team 2: 2, 2, 2, 3, 4.
How many opponents team 1's electric ball can knock down: 3, 2, 1, 1, 1.
The same for team 2: 1, 1, 1, 2, 3.
The shield token's bit of $46 for each player: $10 for team 1's nine, $20 for team 2's.
The electric ball's bit of $46 for each player: $40 for team 1, $80 for team 2.
The goal door's bit of $46 for each end: 8 and 4.
The frame of the arc over a controlled player who has the ball, by his place in the team.
Each player's role for the computer's play (team_mate_ai): 0 goalkeeper, 1 defender, 2 midfielder, 3 centre forward, 4 winger; $FF ends.
Each player's line: 1 defence (with the goalkeeper), 2 midfield, 3 attack, which pass_ball and cover compare.
The group of each squad place for the gym: 0 goalkeeper and defence, 1 midfield, 2 attack, 3 substitutes.
For each of team 1's players, a player of his team (here 0) for team_mate_ai and the transport token ($1CF6,x + 6).
The same for team 2 (9).
Each player's team number: 0 for team 1 ($1D08), 1 for team 2 ($1D11).
Team 2's entries of team_of: 1 for each of its nine players; read with $1D1A in the run-out.
The direction team 2's players walk in during the run-out ($FF to stand), read in turn with $1D23.
The run-out directions for team 1's players.
The goalkeeper's stance frames, by his stance and the end he defends ($AD, $A5, $AE, $A6 ...).
Team 2's players' colour by its team number ($3D, from 0 to 3 by its low two bits): 12, 5, 7 or 6, into player_colours_2 (match_sides).
Team 2's possession colour by its team number: 1, 3, 1 or 3, into possession_colour_2.
Team 2's colour in the panel by its team number: 1, 5, 7 or 6 (panel_colours).

The sprite colours of team 1's nine players (2, red; the goalkeeper is player 0, the first), also team 1's panel colour (panel_colours). The ninth, at $1D48, is also read as team 1's colour with team 2's first at $1D49 (pitch_halves_colour).
Team 1's ninth player's colour (player 8, a winger); pitch_halves_colour reads it and $1D49 as the two teams' colours, indexed by team.
The colours of team 2's nine players, set by match_sides from team_2_colours; the ball's colour (1, white) after them.
The colour of a team 1 player with the ball (4, purple).
The colour of a team 2 player with the ball, set by match_sides from team_2_possession.
Each of team 1's players' column at kick-off; match_sides swaps it with team 2's ($1D5E) when the teams change ends.
Team 2's kick-off columns.
Team 1's kick-off rows.
Team 2's kick-off rows.
The row each of team 1's players starts the run-out from, at his resting column.
Team 2's.
The end each of team 1's players attacks (0) at kick-off; match_sides sets it for each half.
Team 2's ends (1), with the ball's after them.
The left edge of each of team 1's players' area (the formation), in columns; the computer keeps him inside it.
Team 2's left edges.
The top edge of each of team 1's players' area, in rows.
Team 2's top edges.
The right edge of each of team 1's players' area.
Team 2's right edges.
The bottom edge of each of team 1's players' area.
Team 2's bottom edges.
Menu 0's items for run_menu: a count, then column, row and text address for each: 1 PLAYER GAME, 2 PLAYER GAME, DEMO; the texts follow.
